title: Getting started
voice: The narration, one segment per beat of video.mjs, in order. `pad` is the silence after the line before the next beat may start; a beat also waits for its actions to finish.

segments.text: In the next few minutes we'll install exuvia, build a small graph of three nodes, see what runs when one of them changes, put a view on top, and turn on the agent.
Exuvia is one Python package with the web interface inside. To try it without installing anything, put uvx in front of each command. uv downloads exuvia the first time.

exuvia init creates a project, and a project is just a folder: nodes for the steps of the graph, lib for shared Python helpers, views for interfaces, and a pyproject file for the packages your nodes import.

There's already a first node. A node is a Python function with the exuvia node decorator, in a file named after it. This one takes no parameters, so it depends on nothing, and it returns a small table.
Now start the workbench with exuvia serve, and open the address it prints.
Here's the canvas, with our one node, marked new because it has never run. Select it, and its code opens beside the graph. Then run it.
The output is in the Data tab: three rows, and the type of each column. Runs keeps the log of every run.
Leave the server running. It watches the project folder, so a file you change in your own editor shows up here by itself.
Let's add a second node. New node: call it squares. Its input is hello, picked already because hello is selected.
The input is a parameter named hello, and that's the whole dependency declaration: exuvia passes it the output of the hello node. Keep the rows where y is above one, and save.
Nodes can be SQL too. In a SQL node, the nodes upstream are tables, and the query runs in DuckDB. This one counts the rows that survived, and adds them up.
The canvas shows hello, squares, summary. Run summary, and exuvia runs it with every stale node upstream of it, in order.
Two rows survived, with a total of thirteen.
The same works from a terminal, with no interface at all. exuvia run runs whatever is stale. Everything is fresh already, so nothing runs.
Now change something. Every output is stored under a hash of its content, so exuvia can tell exactly what a change affects. Raise the threshold from one to three, and save.
exuvia status says squares is stale because its code changed, and summary because squares is stale.
Run it. Squares ran again, but y above three keeps the same two rows. Its output is identical, so it has the same hash, and summary didn't need to run.
Make the threshold four, and the output is different, so summary runs too.
Both outputs of squares are still on disk, and the code is kept the same way. The History tab has every save, what it changed, and a way back to any of them.

A schedule belongs to a node, not to the whole graph. Give the decorator a cron expression: here, five in the afternoon on weekdays. While the server runs, the node runs on its schedule, and the nodes downstream refresh only if its output changed.

Nodes compute. A view is the interface you put on top of them, and it's front-end code: a folder of React, TypeScript and CSS under views. Let's make one called overview, with the three files from the tutorial.

They show up in the workbench's files. The manifest names the nodes the view may read. The entry file is a React component: use table gives it a node's output, and use query runs SQL over the nodes it reads. The stylesheet uses the workbench's colours, so the view follows light and dark mode.
Open Views at the top of the workbench and pick Overview. There's no build step and nothing to install: exuvia compiles the files in the browser and draws the view in a sandboxed frame.
Change the threshold back to one and run what's stale, and the view redraws with the new rows. A view only reads: it never runs a node itself.

Last, the agent: a model with tools over your project. Give exuvia an API key in the project's dot env file, here one for OpenRouter, and restart the server. exuvia init already keeps dot env out of git.
Then ask for something in the agent panel. Add a node that ranks the rows of squares by y.
Every tool call shows in the conversation, and the nodes the agent touches flash on the canvas.
What it writes are ordinary files in nodes, which you can read, edit and commit like the ones you wrote.
That's the tour. The docs go further: everything a node can declare, run parameters and replays, the whole view API, and hubs that share your projects with your team.
